In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a novel, rapid, non-invasive method for assessing myocardial fibrosis in patients with asymptomatic degenerative MR, using T1 mapping.
the identification of those with truly severe degenerate MR who are most likely to benefit from surgery, and the identification of those who are at risk for poorer outcomes with surgical repair.
the question of how to identify the asymptomatic patient at risk for developing triggers and how best to identify those with severe MR who may benefit from intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the decision to intervene in asymptomatic degenerated MR remains a matter for individual clinical judgement.
the optimal management strategy is unclear, and the choice should be based on the individual characteristics of each patient.

, in the absence of symptoms and LV dysfunction, the decision to intervene or not in the asymptomatic MR patient is based on a number of factors including age, co-morbidities, the presence of atrial fibrillation, the degree of pulmonary hypertension and the degree of LV dysfunction, but also on the patient’s own preference.5 The role of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging in this setting has been limited.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the risk for adverse outcomes is increased in asymptomatic patients who have a higher degree of LV dysfunction, higher regurgitant volume, and higher pulmonary artery pressures and is also increased in patients who have a greater degree of myocardial fibrosis, as measured by T1 mapping.

the presence of myocardial fibrosis on T1 mapping, as assessed by the extracellular volume fraction (ECV) in patients with severe degenerative mitral valve regurgitation (MVR), may predict worse outcome after mitral valve repair.
T1 mapping can be used in asymptomatic degenerate mitral regurgitations to predict LV remodeling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
T1 mapping can help to identify patients who are at risk of developing triggers for intervention.

T1 mapping may help identify patients who have a higher likelihood of fibrosis and, hence, a higher likelihood of developing triggers and/or poorer longer term outcomes, even if they have no symptoms or signs of LV dysfunction.
, in the absence or presence of triggers, the degree of myocardial fibrosis, as assessed with T1 mapping, is a powerful prognostic factor for the development of symptoms or death.
